extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and overcoming pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g) rejections, including rules for affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.131/1.132), derivation, priority/antedating, and perfection of benefit/priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of foreign priority claims (37 CFR 1.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreign priority filing date must antedate the reference and be perfected. The filing date of the priority document is not perfected unless applicant has filed a certified priority document in the application (and an English language translation, if the document is not in English) (see 37 CFR 1.55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If priority was not perfected by timely filing of the certified priority document/translation, survival of the earlier filing date may require filing a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed priority claim under 37 CFR 1.55. See MPEP §§ 213-216 for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 (37 CFR 1.78/1.76)
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 within the time periods set in 37 CFR 1.78: (a) for applications filed on or after September 16, 2012, file an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 which contains a specific reference to a prior application in accordance with 37 CFR 1.78; or (b) for applications filed prior to September 16, 2012, amend the specification to contain a specific reference or file an ADS under 37 CFR 1.76 containing the specific reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, the applicant must establish that the prior application satisfies the enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (for applications filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012) or 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (for earlier filings), or file a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed claim under 37 CFR 1.78.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to use prior application's filing date if benefit not entitled
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing date of a prior application cannot be used to antedate a reference if the application at issue is not entitled to claim the benefit of the prior application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Costello, 717 F.2d 1346, 219 USPQ 389 (Fed. Cir. 1983) for precedent on this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 to overcome pre-AIA 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the reference invention is not by 'another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affidavit/declaration that is only a naked assertion of inventorship and that fails to provide context, explanation or evidence to support the assertion is insufficient (see EmeraChem Holdings, LLC v. Volkswagen Grp. of Am., Inc.). The evidence of record must show who invented the subject matter; declarations should provide context, explanation, and supporting exhibits where possible. See MPEP §§ 715.01(a), 715.01(c), and 716.10 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing a reference describes an inventor's (or joint inventor's) own work
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case based on a patent, U.S. patent application publication, or international application publication may be overcome by showing that the disclosure is a description of the inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own previous work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a showing can be made by proving that the inventor(s) named in the patent/publication was associated with applicant (e.g., same assignee) and learned of the inventor's or at least one joint inventor's invention from the inventor directly or indirectly. In situations where a sole-inventor application precedes a later joint application, it must be proven that the joint invention was made first or otherwise shown by evidence/timeline (see In re Mathews; In re Land).

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to show diligence or reduction to practice when reference is applicant's own work
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference reflects an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work, evidence of diligence or reduction to practice does not need to be provided to establish that the inventor invented the subject matter disclosed in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showing that the reference disclosure arose from the inventor's work coupled with a showing of conception by the inventor before the filing date of the reference will overcome the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection. Submission of an affidavit under 37 CFR 1.132 by the inventor who invented the subject matter is a proper mechanism (see In re DeBaun). Other joint inventors need not submit disclaimers, but if submitted should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims in a reference do not, by themselves, establish inventorship of individual elements or subcombinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of combination claims in a reference is not evidence that the inventor invented individual elements or subcombinations included in that combination if the elements/subcombinations are not separately claimed apart from the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations or affidavits that do not identify the specific species or separate claimed subcombination will be insufficient (see In re DeBaun; In re Facius; In re Mathews). Examiners should require evidence addressing the particular elements at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) — requirement of correct inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) bars issuance of a patent where an applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented; correct inventorship of a claimed invention must be named in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must presume applicants are the proper inventors unless there is evidence of record that another made the invention and that the applicants derived the invention. In an uncommon situation where it is clear the application does not name the correct inventive entity and there has been no request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, the examiner should reject the claims under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) (see In re VerHoef; Pannu v. Iolab Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation requires complete conception and communication enabling one of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation requires complete conception by another and communication of that conception by any means to the party charged with derivation prior to any date on which it can be shown that the charged party possessed knowledge of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The communication of a complete conception must be sufficient to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to construct and successfully operate the invention (Kilbey v. Thiele; Hedgewick v. Akers; Gambro Lundia AB v. Baxter Healthcare Corp.). Examiners and practitioners should focus on whether the communicated information enabled practice of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party alleging derivation does not have to prove actual reduction to practice; derivation not limited to public or domestic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The party alleging derivation need not prove an actual reduction to practice in order to show derivation. Derivation is not limited to public knowledge and the site of derivation need not be in this country to bar a deriver from patenting the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Scott v. Brandenburger and Ex parte Andresen for authority. Evidence of communication and conception sufficient to show derivation is critical even without proof of reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) — requirements for prior art and interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) bars issuance of a patent where another made the invention in the United States before the inventor and had not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it. In determining priority under this subsection, consideration is given to conception dates, reduction to practice, and reasonable diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify as prior art under 102(g) there must be evidence the subject matter was actually reduced to practice; conception alone is not sufficient. Filing an application is a constructive reduction to practice but generally does not provide the evidence necessary to show an actual reduction to practice required for 102(g) in ex parte examination (see Kimberly-Clark; In re Zletz). Subject matter only qualifying under 102(g) may also be used in an obviousness (pre-AIA 103) rejection, subject to exceptions in 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference practice and priority time charts (application of 102(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (g) is the basis of interference practice for determining priority of invention between parties. Interferences are inter partes proceedings to determine which party first invented, considering conception, reduction to practice, and diligence; priority time charts illustrate outcomes based on conception/reduction/diligence sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference practice operates to the exclusion of ex parte practice under 37 CFR 1.131; subject matter which is the basis of an interference is not open to further inquiry under 1.131 during that interference. Lost counts in an interference are not per se statutory prior art, though subject matter available as prior art under pre-AIA 102 may be used under 103 (see In re Deckler). See MPEP Chapter 2300 for interference procedure and priority charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on use of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits (ex parte antedating) vs interference
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.131 permits an inventor to show an actual date of invention prior to the effective date of a reference (to antedate a reference) in ex parte practice, provided the reference is not a statutory bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) or a U.S. patent application publication claiming the same patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, 37 CFR 1.131 does not apply in interference proceedings; interference practice takes precedence and subject matter in an interference is not open to 1.131 inquiry while the interference is ongoing (see Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic requirement for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) prior art — 'made in this country'
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is available only if made in this country. An invention is 'made' when there is a conception and a reduction to practice; publication alone is not a constructive reduction to practice for 102(g) purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of conception, reduction to practice and diligence relied upon for 102(g) must be demonstrated as occurring in the United States (see Kondo v. Martel). Compare case law (Colbert v. Lofdahl) for related contexts.
